title: Melanosome evolution shaped sensory biology and terrestrial adaptations in early aquatic vertebrates
authors: Daniel J. Cirtina; Beatriz Carazo del Hoyo; Shaun P. Collin; Maria E. McNamara
abstract: The photic environment is a key driver of fish ecology that shapes adaptations to aquatic habitats. The evolutionary history of these adaptations, however, is difficult to trace. Melanosomes, melanin-rich organelles, offer unique insights into physiology and ecology and often fossilise. Here, we present a comparative analysis of melanosomes from extant and fossil fishes to trace the evolution of ecological and physiological adaptations through deep time. Melanosomes from internal tissues of extant fishes exhibit highly conserved geometries in all major taxonomic groups examined, indicating persistent functional constraints during evolution. Larger, more abundant melanosomes in lungfish likely reflect adaptations that underpin the vertebrate water-to-land transition. In contrast, eye melanosomes exhibit lineage-specific patterns. Bony fishes possess cylindrical eye melanosomes associated with retinomotor movements, photoreceptor protection, and improved visual acuity, whereas jawless and cartilaginous fishes possess only spheroidal melanosomes, consistent with visual sensitivity and alternative light-regulation strategies including pupillary modulation. These taxonomic differences are preserved in fossils from the late Carboniferous Mazon Creek biota, indicating that links between melanosome morphology and function were established during the early evolutionary history of these lineages in the Ordovician, approximately 445 million years ago. Early innovations in melanin biology uniquely facilitated vertebrate sensory evolution and ecological diversification.
research_question: How did melanosome evolution influence sensory biology and terrestrial adaptations in early aquatic vertebrates?
main_finding: Melanosome morphology is conserved across fish taxa and linked to ecological and physiological adaptations, with distinct patterns in lungfish and eye melanosomes reflecting evolutionary transitions.
novelty: Use of melanosome geometry from extant and fossil fishes to trace deep-time evolution of sensory and ecological adaptations.
broader_significance: Provides unique insights into vertebrate sensory evolution and ecological diversification during the water-to-land transition, based on fossilized cellular structures.
theme: Evolutionary biology and sensory adaptation in aquatic vertebrates

title: Evaluation of vaccine-induced anti-lipopolysaccharide antibodies against clinically relevant Klebsiella pneumoniae strains to inform vaccine design
authors: Robert M. Lawrence; Nathalie Karaky; Emma Bownes; Edward Hildebrand; Cristina Alaimo; Domenico Maione; Francesca Micoli; Kathryn E. Holt; Kelly L. Wyres; David Goldblatt
abstract: Abstract Klebsiella pneumoniae is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis in low- and middle-income countries and is increasingly multi-drug resistant, highlighting the need for vaccines. Putative vaccine targets include the lipopolysaccharide (O antigen) and capsular polysaccharide (K antigen), but capsule may mask O antigen and limit antibody-mediated opsonophagocytosis. We evaluated the activity of O antigen-specific antibodies induced by a tetravalent bioconjugate vaccine against 146 clinical isolates representing 17 prevalent capsule types associated with neonatal sepsis. Susceptibility to antibody-mediated killing varied by capsule type: four were consistently susceptible, six showed heterogeneous responses, and seven were resistant despite remaining susceptible to K antigen-specific antibodies. Killing of susceptible strains was predominantly mediated by anti-O1 antibodies, as demonstrated by competitive inhibition with purified polysaccharides. Collectively, these findings support an antigen-sparing vaccine design strategy, in which susceptible capsule types may be replaced by a single O type, reducing vaccine complexity while maintaining broad functional coverage.
research_question: How effective are vaccine-induced anti-lipopolysaccharide antibodies against diverse Klebsiella pneumoniae strains for vaccine design?
main_finding: Anti-O antigen antibodies show variable killing efficacy depending on capsule type, with some capsule types susceptible and others resistant.
novelty: Identification of capsule-dependent susceptibility to anti-O antigen antibodies and support for antigen-sparing vaccine design.
broader_significance: Findings inform streamlined vaccine strategies targeting prevalent capsule types to combat neonatal sepsis caused by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae.

title: Distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL captured by cryoEM reveal structural principles governing fusion activation
authors: Gonzalo L. González‐Del Pino; Richard M. Walsh; Chanyoung Lee; Hunter C. Russell; Doina Atanasiu; Tina M. Cairns; Wan Ting Saw; Gary H. Cohen; Ekaterina E. Zheleznova Heldwein
abstract: Abstract Orthoherpesviridae infect most humans for life and cause myriad diseases. These viruses distribute cell-entry functions among receptor-binding proteins such as gD, the conserved membrane fusogen gB, and the gH/gL heterodimer, which couples receptor engagement to gB activation. Here, we report cryoEM structures of HSV-2 gH/gL, including complexes with four antibody fragments, in distinct conformational states. Structural analysis suggests that these structures represent pre-activation and intermediate states rather than a post-activation state. Antibody binding appears to shift the gH/gL conformational equilibrium of gH/gL, either stabilizing the pre-activation state or promoting refolding into intermediate or post-activation-like states. Two regions – the N terminus and a domain H2 switch – adopt distinct conformations and may transmit the activating signal from gD to gB. We propose that receptor-bound gD displaces the gH N terminus, initiating allosteric rearrangements that culminate in switch refolding and may help release prefusion gB from an autoinhibited gH/gL-gB complex. Switch conservation suggests that this activation mechanism may be shared across Orthoherpesviridae . These findings uncover structural principles governing gH/gL-mediated activation of membrane fusion.
research_question: What are the distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL and how do they govern fusion activation?
main_finding: CryoEM structures reveal pre-activation and intermediate states of HSV-2 gH/gL and suggest a mechanism for fusion activation involving conformational changes.
novelty: Identification of distinct conformational states of HSV-2 gH/gL and structural insights into the activation mechanism via antibody binding and domain rearrangements.
broader_significance: Provides fundamental understanding of herpesvirus membrane fusion activation, potentially informing antiviral strategies.
theme: Molecular virology and structural biology of viral fusion proteins

title: Organic matter composition modulates its degradation under the combined effects of iron (oxyhydr)oxides and light
authors: Dawei Cai; Yandi Hu; Caroline L. Peacock; Suona Zhang; Xudong Yang; Wen Liu; Peng Zhang; Quan Chen; Bo Pan; Jinren Ni
abstract: The extent of organic matter (OM) degradation in sunlit surface soils and shallow marine sediments is critical to global carbon and nitrogen cycling. Association with iron (oxyhydr)oxides can reduce degradation, but the role of light in iron–OM interaction is underexplored. Here we show that OM composition determines contrasting responses to iron and light. Carboxyl- and/or hydroxyl-containing OM undergoes oxidation and decarboxylation, releasing carbon dioxide, whereas protein-like carboxyl–amine OM forms cross-linked products through condensation and polymerization, with only limited degradation. Iron and light promote oxidation–decarboxylation by enhancing electron transfer and visible-light absorption, while iron promotes protein unfolding and light may provide energy for polymerization. Under high-irradiance conditions equivalent to one-month cumulative daylight exposure, a conditional assessment of representative sunlight-exposed topsoil OM indicates potential carbon losses of ~8% for carboxyl- and/or hydroxyl-type OM versus ~1% for carboxyl–amine-type OM. Photochemically promoted amide formation may limit OM degradation and carbon loss, informing carbon management and process-based carbon cycle models. This study shows that iron minerals and sunlight drive different fates for organic matter in soils and sediments depending on its chemistry: some forms are broken down and lose carbon, while others form cross-linked products that resist degradation.
research_question: How does organic matter composition influence its degradation under combined effects of iron (oxyhydr)oxides and light?
main_finding: Organic matter composition determines contrasting degradation responses to iron and light, with some types undergoing oxidation and carbon loss, while others form resistant cross-linked products.
novelty: Demonstrates that iron minerals and sunlight drive different degradation pathways based on organic matter chemistry, highlighting photochemically promoted amide formation limiting degradation.
broader_significance: Findings inform carbon management and improve process-based carbon cycle models by elucidating how iron and light interactions affect soil and sediment carbon fate.
theme: Carbon cycling and organic matter degradation influenced by mineral-light interactions

title: Dynamically adaptive soft bioelectronics for neuro-immunomodulatory cancer therapy
authors: Wenliang Liu; Jingjie Liu; Renyuan Sun; Ming Yang; Dingke Zhang; Kun Yang; Weixian Xu; Chuan Gao; Shihao Wang; Ziyu Zhang; Qiong Wang; Wenyuan Wang; Qingya Liu; Lei Zhang; Jiexiong Feng
abstract: Abstract Many solid tumors remain refractory to immunotherapy due to profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments. Although vagus nerve stimulation offers a direct neural axis to reprogram immune function, its potential in cancer immunotherapy remains unrealized due to the absence of stable, system-level neuromodulation platforms. Herein, we develop a miniature subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulator (SVNS) for near-organ neuromodulation of pancreatic tumor immunity. To construct stable electrical coupling with subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve (SVN) along the esophagus, a dynamically adaptive neural interface comprising an injectable anti-fatigue adhesive conductive hydrogel and a deformable liquid metal electrode is explored. The SVNS is integrated with a battery-free lead-free wireless power module, which can be configured into a Swiss-roll architecture, enabling minimally invasive implantation. In an orthotopic mouse model of pancreatic tumor, chronic SVN stimulation using SVNS suppressed tumor growth and metastasis, reshaped tumor innervation, promoted a shift toward an M1-like TAM phenotype, enhanced cytotoxic immune cell infiltration, and further potentiated the efficacy of anti-PD-1 immunotherapy.
research_question: Can subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulation modulate pancreatic tumor immunity to enhance cancer immunotherapy?
main_finding: Chronic subdiaphragmatic vagus nerve stimulation suppressed tumor growth and metastasis and enhanced immune response in a pancreatic tumor mouse model.
novelty: Development of a dynamically adaptive, minimally invasive vagus nerve stimulator integrating conductive hydrogel and liquid metal electrodes.
broader_significance: Demonstrates a novel neuromodulation platform that could improve immunotherapy outcomes for solid tumors by reprogramming tumor microenvironments.

title: Differentiating Westerly and Asian monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean since the late Pliocene
authors: Yi Yang; Fei Yu; Jingtao Zhao; Xue Ding; Panfeng Li; Shuang Wang; Xiaoyan Ruan; Xiaoqiang Yang; Thomas J. Algeo; Bangqi Hu; Shucheng Xie
abstract: Asian dust flux is a fundamental regulator of global climate and marine biogeochemical cycles, yet it is difficult to separate the dust fractions delivered to the tropical Pacific Ocean by the Westerlies and East Asian Winter Monsoon (EAWM). We present a 4-million-year record of eolian evolution from the Philippine Sea to deconvolve these two distinct transport systems on the basis of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting. Our results show that the Westerlies component is primarily derived from hyper-arid deserts, whereas the EAWM-driven component originates from the semi-arid margins of East and Central Asia. Of importance is the finding that Westerly-driven transport reflects a coherent response to global cooling and hemispheric thermal gradients, whilst the Asia monsoon contribution is mediated by vegetation cover. We further demonstrate that hydroclimatic fluctuations in EAWM marginal zones modulate dust availability through vegetation-induced surface roughness and pedogenic refinement, resulting in a pronounced non-linear relationship between dust flux and wind energetics. This suggests the ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus the tropical ocean, necessitating integration of dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape interventions on dust into Earth System Models to predict global carbon cycling in a warming world. “Ecological conditions of dust source regions exert an impact on dust flux and thus on the tropical ocean, shown using grain size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting of a 4-million-year-long sediment record from the Philippine Sea”
research_question: How can Westerly and East Asian Winter Monsoon dust fluxes to the tropical Pacific Ocean be differentiated over the last 4 million years?
main_finding: Westerly dust originates from hyper-arid deserts and responds to global cooling, while Asian monsoon dust comes from semi-arid margins influenced by vegetation cover, showing a nonlinear relationship with wind energetics.
novelty: Use of grain-size modeling and geochemical fingerprinting to deconvolve two distinct dust transport systems over a 4-million-year record.
broader_significance: Highlights the need to integrate dynamic vegetation impacts and anthropogenic landscape changes on dust flux into Earth System Models to improve predictions of global carbon cycling under climate change.
theme: Climate impacts of dust flux and Earth System modeling

title: An Early Jurassic soft eggshell provides insights into the evolutionary history of dinosaur eggs
authors: Zhiyong Di; Haiquan Wang; Tao Wang; Z H Dong; Xiaoli Li; Feng Zhang; Xiaoguang Li; Heyv Lv; Tianyu Ai
abstract: Early eggshell fossils offer invaluable insights into evolutionary innovations in over 300 million years of amniote egg history. However, the incompleteness of the dinosaur eggshell fossil record hinders ancestral state reconstruction and leads to uncertainty about whether the first dinosaur egg was soft-shelled, semi-rigid-shelled, or rigid-shelled. Herein, we present a fossilized soft eggshell (Mutabilisoolithus dawaensis) from an Early Jurassic basal sauropodomorph. We find that M. dawaensis has a soft, plastic-like deformation, a thick cuticle, a thin calcareous layer formed by non-interlocking shell units, and a significantly thick shell membrane. Its shell membrane is similar to that of avian eggs in structure, diameter, and arrangement of the fibers, as well as in the distinctions among outer, inner, and limiting membrane layers, but it is much thicker than that of avian eggs. In dinosaurian egg evolutionary history, M. dawaensis provides evidence of early Jurassic soft-shelled eggs, may represent the earliest stage of biomineralization, and bridges the gap between non-biomineralized membranous soft eggshells and biomineralized semi-rigid eggshells. Fossil dinosaur eggs are extremely rare, and there is uncertainty about their ancestral anatomy and evolution. A newly described Early Jurassic sauropodomorph soft-shelled egg offers valuable insights into the reproductive biology of dinosaurs.
research_question: What are the characteristics and evolutionary significance of Early Jurassic soft dinosaur eggshells?
main_finding: Discovery of a fossilized soft eggshell from an Early Jurassic basal sauropodomorph showing features bridging non-biomineralized and biomineralized eggshells.
novelty: First evidence of Early Jurassic soft-shelled dinosaur eggs providing insights into early biomineralization stages.
broader_significance: Improves understanding of dinosaur reproductive biology and evolutionary history of eggshell biomineralization.
theme: Paleontology and evolutionary biology of dinosaur eggshells

title: Programmable roll-to-roll laser processing for high value application of low-grade carbon fiber materials
authors: Guangmeng Chen; Wenjie Yu; 江广华; Li Jia; Ziqiang Hu; Weiwei Zhao; Xiaosu Yi; Xiaoqing Liu
abstract: Abstract Growing production of carbon fibers generates substantial short-chopped fibers that are difficult for high-value use due to their structural discontinuity. Carbon fiber felts offer potential, yet weak inter-fiber bonding and poor conductivity limit the performance. We report a roll‑to‑roll laser processing strategy that uses a liquid precursor to form laser‑induced graphene at fiber‑fiber interfaces, creating conductive pathways and mechanical interconnections. This approach increases tensile strength from 4.1 to 32.2 MPa and electrical conductivity from 1224.0 to 15151.5 S/m. The resulting films demonstrate efficient electrothermal de‑icing and, after copper deposition, lightning strike protection with a damage area of 9657 mm² and depth of 0.4 mm, comparable to aluminum mesh but with 15% lower weight. A custom‑built laser platform enables scalable production. Here, we show the conversion of low‑grade carbon fibers into lightweight, functional films for aerospace applications via scalable laser processing.
query: energy storage flexibility; renewable energy land use
research_question: Can roll-to-roll laser processing improve the mechanical and electrical properties of low-grade carbon fiber materials?
main_finding: Laser processing with a liquid precursor forms conductive graphene pathways, significantly enhancing tensile strength and conductivity of carbon fiber felts.
novelty: Use of scalable roll-to-roll laser processing to convert low-grade carbon fibers into high-performance, lightweight films with improved bonding and conductivity.
broader_significance: Enables high-value applications of abundant low-grade carbon fibers, potentially reducing material waste and advancing lightweight functional materials for aerospace.
theme: Advanced materials processing for enhanced carbon fiber performance

title: Single-atom-doped zeolite electrolyte for quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries
authors: Lutong Shan; Fulong Li; Zixuan Wang; Zhenyue Xing; Shan Guo; Tsung‐Yi Chen; Wei‐Hsiang Huang; Xiaodong Shi; Xinlong Tian; Guanzhou Zhu
abstract: Quasi-solid electrolytes can mitigate polyiodide shuttling and suppress parasitic reactions at zinc negative electrode in zinc-iodine batteries by reducing free water, but their limited liquid content often results in sluggish interfacial charge transfer. Here we show liquid-electrolyte-wetted quasi-solid electrolytes by combining single-atom-modified zeolites (single-atom = iron, cobalt, nickel, and copper) with zinc sulfate aqueous solution for high-rate zinc-iodine batteries. Theoretical calculations, in situ spectroscopy, and laser confocal microscopy reveal that the single-atom metal sites enhance iodine conversion kinetics and suppress polyiodide shuttling through a synergistic catalytic-adsorption effect, with iron-doped zeolite exhibiting the strongest performance. Iron-doped zeolite further stabilizes water molecules, suppresses side reactions, and promotes uniform zinc deposition. The iron-doped zeolite-assembled zinc-iodine batteries maintain a discharge capacity of 81.2 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) after 6,800 cycles at 4 A g−1, while proof-of-concept pouch cells exhibit a capacity of 147.6 mAh g−1 (based on iodine mass) or 52 mAh g−1 (based on total positive electrode mass) after 200 cycles at 0.5 A g−1. Lastly, iron-doped zeolite also demonstrates compatibility with other positive electrode materials for rechargeable zinc batteries. Quasi-solid zinc iodine batteries face sluggish kinetics due to low liquid content. Here, authors report single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes that simultaneously catalyze iodine conversion, suppress polyiodide shuttling, and stabilize zinc deposition, achieving 6,800 stable cycles at high rates and demonstrating proof-of-concept pouch-cell performance.
research_question: Can single-atom-doped zeolite electrolytes improve performance and stability of quasi-solid-state zinc-iodine batteries?
main_finding: Single-atom metal-doped zeolite electrolytes enhance iodine conversion kinetics, suppress polyiodide shuttling, stabilize zinc deposition, and enable long cycle life at high rates.
novelty: Use of single-atom-modified zeolites to simultaneously catalyze iodine conversion and stabilize zinc deposition in quasi-solid electrolytes.
broader_significance: Improves zinc-iodine battery performance and stability, advancing quasi-solid-state battery technology for safer, high-rate energy storage.
theme: Energy storage materials and battery technology

title: Molecular insights into GPR55 modulation reveal an atypical activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent efficacy regulation
authors: Tobias Claff; Chamalee Demalgiriya-Gamage; Andhika Bintang Mahardhika; Nikolaos Angelos Stamos; Frederik Bangnowski; Xue Sun; Katharina L. Duerr; Carol V. Robinson; Rainer Haney; Lee Frego; Herbert Nar; Christa Elisabeth Müller; Rebecca Ebenhoch; Jörg Thomas Kley; Dietmar Weichert
abstract: GPR55 is a lipid-activated G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) implicated in metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration. Lysophosphatidylinositol (LPI) species are proposed as endogenous agonists, but progress in understanding GPR55 function has still been limited by suboptimal chemical probes. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of GPR55 in both inactive and active states. The inactive-state structure bound to the inverse agonist CID16020046 facilitated the rational design of an improved in vitro tool compound, BI-8310. Surprisingly, mutation of a glycosylation site in extracellular loop 2 converted CID16020046 into a potent agonist, enabling co-structure determination of the active, G13-bound receptor. Comparative analysis of both states bound to the same ligand provides insights into an atypical activation mechanism that diverges from the typical helix VI outward movement observed in other GPCRs. Functional mutagenesis, N-glycoproteomics, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) substantiate the findings. These results establish a basis for targeted modulation of GPR55 in pathophysiological conditions. GPR55 is a lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor. Here, authors present cryo-EM structures of inactive and active states of GPR55, revealing an atypical activation mechanism with a glycosylation-dependent switch in ligand efficacy.
research_question: How does GPR55 activation and glycosylation regulate ligand efficacy at the molecular level?
main_finding: Cryo-EM structures reveal an atypical GPR55 activation mechanism and glycosylation-dependent switch converting an inverse agonist into a potent agonist.
novelty: First structural elucidation of inactive and active GPR55 states showing unique activation distinct from typical GPCRs and glycosylation-dependent ligand efficacy modulation.
broader_significance: Provides molecular basis for targeted modulation of GPR55 in diseases related to metabolism, inflammation, and neurodegeneration.

title: In the synthetic biology era, engineered fungi could mitigate carbon dioxide emissions and enhance environmental resilience
authors: Kyle Davis; Joanna Tannous
abstract: Abstract Over the past two decades, there has been a staggering increase in greenhouse gas emissions, particularly carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) from unrestrained anthropogenic activities, leading to notable environmental shifts. Despite continuous efforts to reduce emissions, the world is not making satisfactory progress, which calls for immediate action to implement alternative strategies to enhance environmental sustainability. The Earth naturally absorbs and stores carbon through various processes, but merely keeping pace with ongoing human activities is no longer sufficient. Land plants and marine prokaryotes absorb CO 2 during photosynthesis and store carbon as biomass. Eukaryotic organisms also represent a valuable resource that can provide insights into the biological fixation and removal of atmospheric CO 2 . Expanding the capacities of Earth’s natural systems offers enormous potential for enhancing carbon sinks and promoting environmental resilience. Although extensive synthetic engineering of plant systems has been conducted to enhance their native carbon fixation pathways, research on microorganisms, especially fungi, has been limited. In this review, we specifically explore the role of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, elucidating their responses to environmental shifts and their potential for climate change mitigation. We place particular emphasis on the role of various fungal guilds in this process, highlighting those that should be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications. We then engage with previous endeavors to address primary challenges in advancing genetic tools for these understudied fungi. Lastly, we discuss how integrating synthetic biology practices into the field of soil-associated fungi can drive advances in long-term carbon storage, enhance degradation of environmental pollutants, and improve nutrient exchange and soil health, contributing to more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions. Rising carbon dioxide emissions from human activities are driving environmental change and increasing the need for strategies that strengthen natural carbon sinks and ecosystem resilience. While plants and microorganisms play important roles in carbon capture and storage, the potential of soil-associated fungi remains comparatively underexplored, particularly from a synthetic biology perspective. In this Review, we examine the roles of soil-borne fungi in carbon management, their responses to environmental change, and their potential contributions to climate change mitigation. We highlight key fungal guilds that could be prioritized for future synthetic biology applications and discuss current challenges in developing genetic tools for understudied fungi. Finally, we explore how engineering soil-associated fungi could support long-term carbon storage while providing broader environmental benefits, including pollutant degradation, nutrient exchange, and improved soil health. Together, these opportunities position fungal synthetic biology as a promising approach for developing more resilient soil ecosystems and sustainable environmental interventions.

title: Exsolution of metal nanoparticles by control of point defects
authors: Andreas Rosnes; Bo Jiang; Holger von Wenckstern; Øystein Prytz; Jonathan M. Polfus
abstract: Abstract Exsolution involves redox precipitation of metal nanoparticles from metal oxides, resulting in materials that exhibit excellent electrocatalytic properties and hold great promise for novel types of nanoscale heterostructures. However, a coherent understanding of the phenomenon is lacking. Here, exsolution is described by three point defect equations involving the reduction of the host oxide, reduction and exsolution of the transition metal, and annihilation of host unit cells. Guided by their predictions, significantly enhanced exsolution in terms of molar amount, rate, and nucleation density is achieved by acceptor substitution in the system La 0.2 Ca 0.7 Ti 0.95 Cu 0.05 O 3− δ , as shown by atomic scale imaging and in situ X-ray diffraction and spectroscopy. It is demonstrated that the oxygen stoichiometry of the parent oxide increases upon exsolution despite oxygen loss in the reducing environment. Furthermore, strain in both the host oxide and the exsolved metal can constitute an additional thermodynamic barrier for exsolution beyond the availability of the required point defects.

title: Designing rigid protein fiducials to visualize GPCR conformational states
authors: Alina Vo Vo; Yuan-En Sun; Justin G. English; Michael J. Robertson
abstract: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) mediate precise ligand-specific signaling profiles, yet structural visualization of how ligands alter receptor conformational landscapes in the absence of signaling partners or mimetics has proven challenging. Here we show that by combining generative protein design with deep-learning based ensemble prediction we can reliably design fiducial markers to facilitate cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM) of GPCRs at arbitrary fusion points, enabling the visualization of previously intractable states. We validate the approach with high-throughput determination of inactive state structures of four pharmaceutically relevant GPCRs, allowing for key details of receptor pharmacology to be resolved in each case. We then engineered an extracellular fiducial marker for the prototypical β2-adrenergic receptor that enabled direct structural characterization of the rearrangement of key intracellular motifs in the absence of G-protein. Comparison with recent co-folding models highlights major gaps in current methods for predicting ligand-induced GPCR conformations. These results present a generalizable framework for accessing traditionally inaccessible structural states of small, dynamic proteins. Visualizing how drugs reshape GPCR receptors by cryo-EM has been difficult for many conformational states. Here, authors use designed protein fiducials to image elusive GPCR states, revealing details of ligand induced receptor activation.

title: Coupled sea-level and biodiversity dynamics during the Cambrian SPICE event
authors: Meng Wang; Yukun Shi; Aihua Yang; Haotian Zhang; Xiaoyu Zhang; Yujing Wu; yujie shi; Jianbo Liu; Ren Wei; Zhijun Jin; Mingsong Li
abstract: The prominent Cambrian Steptoean Positive Carbon Isotope Excursion (SPICE) stands as one of Earth’s largest carbon cycle perturbations, marked by widespread marine anoxia, climatic upheaval, and biotic turnover, yet the complete extent and interplay of these environmental changes remain unclear. Here, we integrate high-resolution astrochronology, carbonate carbon isotope records from the North China Block and marine species richness to investigate sedimentary and biogeochemical responses during the SPICE interval. Time series analysis reveals a distinct ~2-million-year sedimentary rhythm that aligns with cycles in reconstructed sea-level fluctuations and biodiversity dynamics. We show that sea-level changes preceded shifts in benthic species richness by 70 kyr, linking astronomically paced eustatic oscillations to marine redox fluctuations and concurrent biodiversity turnover. These findings establish pivotal constraints on ocean-climate interactions during this critical interval, elucidating Earth system resilience to extreme climatic and biogeochemical perturbations. Using astrochronology, Wang et al. estimate that relative sea-level change led benthic turnover by ~70,000 years during the late Cambrian SPICE event under their age model, supporting links among orbital forcing, marine anoxia and biodiversity loss.

title: An integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture with Cu dual active-sites for all-solid-state Li–CO2 batteries
authors: Yunyun Xu; Dashuai Wang; Yuejiao Li; Haifeng Qi; Zhuobin Guo; Tasmia Azam; Pratteek Das; Zhong‐Shuai Wu; Hui–Ming Cheng
abstract: All-solid-state Li–CO2 batteries are limited by sluggish interfacial CO2 redox kinetics and the incomplete decomposition of insulating Li2CO3 at rigid solid-solid-gas interfaces. Here, we report an integrated cathode-electrolyte architecture in which copper atomic clusters and single atoms are co-anchored on freestanding N-doped carbon nanotubes and coupled with a succinonitrile/Li1+xAlyGe2-y(PO4)3-based solid-state electrolyte. The conformal ion-conducting phase and conductive nanotube scaffold provide coupled pathways for Li+, electrons and CO2 at the cathode interface. Electronic coupling between the copper atomic clusters and single atoms induces charge transfer from the former to the latter (~0.457 e−), rendering the Cu cluster sites partially cationic and facilitating the activation of carbonate intermediates. This dual-site configuration changes the discharge pathway and lowers the reaction energy of the rate-determining step to 2.412 eV. The assembled battery delivers a discharge capacity of 21356 mAh g−1 at 200 mA g−1 and operates for 260 cycles (>1000 h) at 500 mA g−1 with an energy efficiency of 78%. This work provides an interfacial design strategy for solid-state Li–CO2 batteries by coupling continuous transport pathways with electronically regulated dual Cu active sites. Stimuli responsive assemblies can offer precise control over behaviour, but use of gases for this control is rare. Here, the authors report the use of carbon dioxide for tuneable nanoparticle response, directed by changes in peptide structure.

title: A synaptic mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complex organizes photoreceptor neurotransmission
authors: Fenglan Wang; Wenna Zhao; Xin Lin; Xiaotian Bian; Qingwen Yang; Zhongqun Chen; Fang He; Xiaoqing Liu; Yu Xi; Bilin Rao; Jun Cao; Jun Zhang; Jia Qu
abstract: Photoreceptor synapses rely on mitochondria, synaptic ribbons, and vesicles, yet how these elements integrate into functional units remains unclear. Here we show, using focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) and electrophysiology, that they form synaptic mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complexes (sMRVcs) with fundamentally different architectures in rods and cones. Rod spherules exhibit a strict 1:1 pairing of a single megamitochondrion with one ribbon, sustaining continuous glutamate release in darkness, whereas cone pedicles contain multiple distributed sMRVcs. Disrupting the mitochondrial anchor protein syntaphilin shifts this ratio to 2:1 in rods, with additional mitochondria recruited near the ribbon, and enhances synaptic transmission. In a retinal degeneration model, the sMRVc progressively disassembles before functional decline, with fragmented mitochondria, detached ribbons, and dispersed vesicles. We also identify non-ribbon release sites selectively targeting horizontal cells. These findings establish the sMRVc as a conserved structural–metabolic module whose subtype-specific organization reflects distinct visual demands and whose integrity is essential for synaptic health. Researchers find photoreceptor synapses contain mitochondrion–ribbon–vesicle complexes: rods have a 1:1 megamitochondrion–ribbon pair; cones have distributed units. Disrupting mitochondrial anchoring shifts rods to 2:1 and boosts signaling, while degeneration breaks the complex apart.
query: water energy nexus; energy storage flexibility

title: ZEB1 maintains energy metabolism to sustain cardiac function through synergistic regulation with TEAD1
authors: Taiwei Chen; Zhinan Wu; Fei Liao; Yiwen Shen; Zhimin Wang; Yuxuan Qian; Guqing Luo; Wenyi Xu; Xinjie He; Yue Huang; Jiyuan Chen; Bihe Xu; Song Z. Ding; Jun Pu
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming plays a critical role in heart failure (HF), but its regulatory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1), a transcription factor initially identified as a regulator of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, has recently been implicated in metabolic regulation. Here, we show that ZEB1 expression is reduced in failing cardiomyocytes. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Zeb1 leads to progressive HF with impaired glycolysis and fatty acid metabolism. Mechanistically, ZEB1 interacts with TEA domain transcription factor 1 (TEAD1) to activate metabolic genes, including pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme 1 (PKM1) and acetyl-CoA acyltransferase 2 (ACAA2), which regulate glycolysis and fatty acid β-oxidation, respectively. Loss of Acaa2 aggravates stress-induced cardiac hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. Acetate supplementation restores cardiac function in Zeb1-deficient mice, whereas ZEB1 overexpression improves pressure overload- and doxorubicin-induced HF. These findings identify the ZEB1-TEAD1 axis as a regulator of cardiac metabolic homeostasis and a potential therapeutic target for HF. Heart failure is a major health challenge, and the mechanisms driving metabolic dysfunction in the failing heart remain poorly understood. Here, the authors show that ZEB1-TEAD1 signaling preserves cardiac energy metabolism and that restoring ZEB1 or supplementing its downstream metabolite acetate mitigates heart failure progression.

title: Persistent seasonal deoxygenation alters benthic metabolic processes and accelerates hypoxia feedbacks in the Baltic Sea
authors: Shuba Varshini Alampalli; Stefanie Böhnke-Brandt; Nicole Adam-Beyer; Katja Laufer; Klaus Wallmann; Hermann W. Bange; Helmke Hepach; Matthias Thiele; Florian Scholz; Emanuel Wyler; M Landthaler; Isabel Diercks; Janina Fuß; Mirjam Perner
abstract: Abstract Nutrient enrichment and warming cause widespread costal deoxygenation, leading to hypoxia or even anoxia in bottom waters. The benthic-water-column-feedbacks that develop under persistent seasonal oxygen depletion and amplify hypoxia remain poorly constrained. A 15-month study of a seasonally hypoxic to anoxic costal system in the southwestern Baltic Sea combined water-column monitoring, sediment chemistry, metabolic rates and microbial analyses with historic data to reveal pronounced seasonal shifts in sediment processes. During winter oxygenation, organic matter degradation, fermentation, aerobic respiration, nitrate- and iron-reduction and microbial competition increased. Re-ventilation following anoxia did not reset sediment biogeochemistry, but initiated intensified oxygen consumption, microbial biosynthetic activity and anaerobic carbon re-cycling. Reactive ironoxyhydroxides became exhausted, the sulfidic zone shoaled and sulfate reduction and pyrite formation rates increased through fall. These processes reinforced benthic feedbacks, progressively reducing the sediment’s capacity to retain sulfide over years. This weakening of sedimentary resilience exacerbates sulfide accumulation in eutrophic costal environments with growing chances of sulfidic deep-water upwelling.

title: Low-carbon technologies support energy security by buffering energy price shocks
authors: Jose A. Ordonez; Matthias Weitzel; Camille Van der Vorst; Rafael Garaffa
abstract: Energy supply crises matter because their economic impacts extend beyond energy markets. We argue that energy security should be understood by how energy systems transmit price shocks to the wider economy. Low-carbon technologies matter because, unlike fossil fuels, they dampen this transmission through the economy. title: Coupled responses of aboveground and belowground net primary productivity stability to nitrogen deposition in grasslands
authors: yaodan zhang; Siyuan Gao; Xinxin Wang; Huiying Liu
abstract: Abstract The temporal stability of plant net primary productivity (NPP), defined as the ratio of temporal mean productivity to its standard deviation, is crucial for sustaining ecosystem services. Yet, little is known about whether the effects of nitrogen deposition on aboveground NPP (ANPP) stability are coupled with corresponding changes in belowground systems. Here we conducted a global meta-analysis based on 542 multi-year observations from 111 studies to assess the impacts of nitrogen deposition on the stability of ANPP and belowground NPP (BNPP). Nitrogen addition significantly decreased the stability of both ANPP and BNPP in a synchronized manner, reflecting a coupled response resulting from the allocation trade-off between mean ANPP and BNPP and their synchronized increase in variability. Further analysis showed that the declines in both ANPP and BNPP stability were associated with decreased plant species richness under nitrogen addition. Moreover, the negative responses intensified with longer treatment durations and higher nitrogen addition intensity. These findings highlight the importance of considering above- and below-ground interactions in future ecosystem management strategies under global change scenarios.

title: Climate-driven water stress in the United States is seasonal, regional, and shaped by adaptation
authors: Joey Blumberg; Travis Warziniack
abstract: This study quantifies drivers of water use across the food-energy-water nexus and assesses how climate change, population growth, and adaptation may reshape future water scarcity in the United States. Using high frequency water withdrawal data from 2000–2020, we disentangle the effects of climate, hydrology, and socioeconomic factors on public water use, crop irrigation, and cooling for thermoelectric power generation. Future water demands (2040–2070) are estimated using recent climate and socioeconomic projections, representing 1.0 ∘C to 2.9 ∘C warming and population growth ranging from 1% to 44%. Across 28 scenarios, we estimate annual water use changes ranging from -10.7% to +28.9% for public use, +32.1% to +43.6% for crop irrigation, and -27.9% to -19.9% for thermoelectric power cooling, contingent on continued adaptive efforts. Results reveal strong sectoral variation in climate sensitivity, seasonal mismatches between water supply and demand, and shifts in regional water stress under future warming. Climate change and economic activity are reshaping when and where water stress occurs in the United States. This study identifies the drivers and locations of water stress and shows how targeted water management policies can reduce future scarcity.

title: Chemistry-infused bandit framework for interpretable autonomous campaign of electrocatalysis
authors: Yi-An Lai; Muxin Xiong; Jingwen Sun; Aijian Huang; Max Van Fleet; Hongyuan Sheng; J A Kim; Felisha Kuo; Tai Ying Lai; Xuian-Rou Lin; Yuehua Chen; Weitong Zhang; Hao Ming Chen; Chong Liu
abstract: Abstract Autonomous experimentation offers a time-efficient route towards accelerated catalyst discovery, but current practices often rely on black-box models that are difficult to interpret. Here we demonstrate the paradigm of interpretable autonomous exploration of a 12-dimensional space in the electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction by integrating an interpretable decision-making artificial intelligence with a fully automated electrochemical platform. Guided by a human’s chemistry-informed hypothesis, a chemistry-infused bandit is established to reflect the locally quadratic approximation between synthetic conditions and electrocatalytic activities near the explored optimum region. Not only does such a decision-making bandit lead to the discovery of previously unreported, earth-abundant electrocatalysts at least comparable to Pt-based ones, the bandit also reveals model-derived hypothesis for how synthetic conditions affect the electrocatalysts’ performance near the identified local optima as autonomous inquiry proceeds, which is otherwise untenable from black-box ones. Incorporating chemistry-informed hypothesis into the decision-making bandit is generally applicable to any chemistry problem and offers a framework for autonomous investigation, advancing hypothesis generation for catalyst’s design principles beyond simple optimization.

title: Water in kimberlitic olivine provides insights into kimberlite ascent and diamond transport
authors: Soumendu Sarkar; Rondi M. Davies; Qiwei Zhang; Luísa D.V. Carvalho; Thomas Stachel; David Graham Pearson
abstract: Kimberlites are volatile-rich magmas that transport diamonds from the deep lithosphere to the surface, yet the exact processes controlling their variable diamond abundances remain debated. Compiled dataset of water contents in mantle olivine shows that kimberlites containing water-rich (>40 wt. ppm) olivine exhibit higher diamond grades. Diffusion modeling coupled with estimates of the ascent velocities of olivine xenocrysts indicate that preserved water in the cores of olivine crystals reflects variable magma ascent rates. High water contents are indicative of rapid ascent that not only limits hydrogen loss but also leads to enhanced diamond transport. Conversely, slower ascent promotes olivine dehydration and reduction in diamond-carrying capacity. The link between olivine water content and diamond grade highlights that ascent rate is a key factor in controlling the varied diamond abundance in kimberlites. Water in olivine thus provides an additional, complementary, and cost-effective proxy for estimating kimberlite ascent and diamond-carrying efficiency. This study links higher diamond grades in kimberlites to water-rich olivine. Modeling suggests that rapid magma ascent preserves higher olivine water contents and facilitates efficient diamond transport, highlighting ascent rate as a key control on diamond preservation.

title: Observation of inherent chiral Smith–Purcell effect via symmetry breaking
authors: Juan‐Feng Zhu; Fei Chen; Jun-Xuan Chen; Junkang Shan; Ayan Nussupbekov; Febiana Tjiptoharsono; Xuan Dong; Mu Wang; Cheng-Wei Qiu; Zhaogang Dong; Ruwen Peng; Lin Wu
abstract: The Smith–Purcell effect arises when charged particles move near a periodic structure, emitting radiation. Conventional approaches for generating chiral Smith–Purcell radiation rely on metasurface phase engineering or resonant mode interference, typically producing narrow-band, weakly chiral emission. Here, we introduce a resonance-interference-free mechanism that leverages the properties of the charged particles themselves. Using a non-chiral, non-resonant silicon grating, we demonstrate broadband, tunable Smith–Purcell radiation with high chirality, achieving a record-high degree of polarization of 0.87. This is enabled by converting the transverse spin angular momentum of electron-induced evanescent waves into a longitudinal form, producing opposite chirality at different azimuthal angles. Beam twisting or displacement offers precise control over chirality, paving the way for compact chiral light sources, advanced X-ray imaging, and integrated particle diagnostics platforms. Existing approaches for generating chiral Smith–Purcell radiation remain limited. Here, the authors overcome these limitations by uncovering the inherent chirality of the Smith–Purcell effect using non-chiral, non-resonant silicon gratings. By controlling the electron–grating configuration, this chirality can be selectively manipulated to produce tunable and highly chiral polarized radiation.

title: Non-polar surface passivation of PbS Quantum Dots using metal thiolates enables photodiodes rivaling InGaAs performance
authors: Debranjan Mandal; Yongjie Wang; Carmelita Rodà; Miguel Dosil; Gaurav Kumar; Lucheng Peng; Gerasimos Konstantatos
abstract: Abstract Colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) short-wave infrared (SWIR) detectors (1-2 µm) are of great interest for a plethora of applications including autonomous driving, machine vision, night and adverse weather imaging, in view of their low-cost and compatibility to read-out electronics. However, to date, CQDs photodetectors still suffer from high dark current and thereby noise such that their performance remains inferior to epitaxially grown III-V semiconductors. This performance gap originates from the limited passivation of non-polar surfaces existent in large PbS CQDs needed to access the SWIR spectral range. Here we report on a lead-thiolate based chemistry that serves to passivate both polar and non-polar surfaces of PbS CQDs yielding inks with unprecedented optoelectronic quality evidenced by open circuit voltage deficit and dark current activation energies matching those of single crystalline semiconductors. As a result, we demonstrate infrared photodetectors with remarkable thermal resilience, very low dark current density ( ~ 34 nA cm −2 at −1 V) and a specific detectivity D* of ~8×10 12 Jones. The measured D* value is on par with that of commercially available InGaAs photodiodes (PDs).

title: Heatwave-induced capacity bottlenecks in European electricity grids
authors: Enming Liang; Minghua Chen; Srinivasan Keshav
abstract: Abstract Heatwaves are becoming more frequent, intense and prolonged as the climate warms, placing stress on the electricity infrastructure underpinning modern societies. Yet how rising temperatures erode grid capacity remains under-quantified. Existing power-flow models either oversimplify thermal effects or become computationally intractable when resolving them in detail. Here we introduce a unified, computationally efficient framework that jointly captures temperature-dependent demand, generator derating and spatially resolved transmission-line thermal limits within an alternating-current optimal power-flow formulation. Applying it to the Western European system with open-access grid, high-resolution weather reanalysis and demand data, we simulate hundreds of projected heatwave scenarios for 2026–2030. Across these represented grid configurations, the analysis reveals substantial national disparities: the Spanish grid exhibits temperature-induced bottlenecks and load shedding, whereas the German grid remains comparatively resilient. Heatwave-aware power-flow analysis thus uncovers structural bottlenecks and should be integrated into grid planning and adaptation as heatwaves intensify under climate change.

title: Determining depth-resolved spatial distribution of solid–electrolyte interphase using non-destructive angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for lithium-metal batteries
authors: Giulio D’Acunto; Sanzeeda Baig Shuchi; Yi Cui; Stacey F. Bent
abstract: The solid electrolyte interphase is a key performance regulator in Li-metal batteries, which are regarded as an important technology for future energy storage. Understanding this crucial interphase through non-destructive analysis is essential to advance the performance and lifespan of Li-metal batteries. We introduce angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy as a non-destructive technique for the depth-profile analysis of the solid electrolyte interphase in Li-metal batteries. Importantly, we show that this characterization technique displays a distinct advantage in preserving the solid electrolyte interphase's integrity compared to traditional sputtering-based depth-profiling. Our findings add to the understanding of compositional differences in the solid electrolyte interphase before the onset of Li electrodeposition and after Li plating. Moreover, we find significant variations in the thickness and distribution of solid electrolyte interphase species across different classes of electrolytes, which strongly influence the solid electrolyte interphase's protective properties and, by extension, Li-metal battery performance. This study benchmarks the application of angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy in revealing detailed, depth-resolved chemical composition of the solid electrolyte interphase in a non-destructive approach. Understanding the solid–electrolyte interphase formed on lithium is vital for improving the lifetime of lithium metal batteries. Here, authors show that angle-resolved X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy can reveal the depth-dependent composition of the interfacial layer without damaging it by ion sputtering.

title: Canadian lakes show contrasting phosphorus trends across climatic regions
authors: Hongwei Guo; Jinhui Jeanne Huang‬‬‬‬; Yunlin Zhang; John P. Smol; Xiaotong Zhu; Ling Jiang; Longwei Li; Weipeng Lin; Han Zhang; Lunche Wang
abstract: Phosphorus regulates lake productivity and water quality, yet long-term changes in lake phosphorus and their climatic drivers remain poorly understood at continental scales. Here we show how total phosphorus changes across 15,240 Canadian lakes > 5 km2 from 1984 to 2025 using a deep neural network trained with 35,452 field measurements and applied to 386,727 Landsat images. Arctic tundra watersheds show increasing phosphorus concentrations of 0.15 μg/L yr−1, whereas boreal forest, temperate forest, agricultural and urban watersheds show declines of 0.07, 0.11, 0.16 and 0.12 μg/L yr−1, respectively. Path analyses link northern increases to ground warming and soil erosion, consistent with permafrost-related phosphorus mobilization. Southern declines are associated with vegetation greening, hydrological change, and reduced human phosphorus inputs, while surface runoff remains important in agricultural and urban systems. These findings reveal contrasting climate-sensitive phosphorus trajectories and show that climate change can reinforce or counteract nutrient management gains, highlighting the need to integrate region-specific climate adaptation into lake management. Lake phosphorus increased in Arctic Canada but declined across other climatic regions, with northern increases linked to ground warming and soil erosion, according to a study that combined field measurements with deep learning analysis of Landsat imagery from 15,240 lakes between 1984 and 2025.

title: A porous solid electrolyte interface enables efficient electroreduction of captured carbon to CO
authors: Shanhe Gong; Qing Xia; Yanjie Zhai; Weisong Li; Jie Wu; Yingying Zhou; Yucong Liao; Kuang Zhu; Yuchen Yang; Yile Yang; Xiaojie She; Zhaolong Wang; Huaming Li; Xiao Zhang; Shu Ping Lau
abstract: Direct electrochemical conversion of captured carbon species offers a route to avoid the energy-intensive steps of thermal CO2 release, compression and transport in conventional carbon capture and utilization. In proton exchange membrane (PEM) reactors, however, the acidic cathode environment promotes hydrogen evolution and limits CO2 regeneration from (bi)carbonate capture media, resulting in low carbon utilization and high energy demand. Here we show a modular PEM–porous solid electrolyte (PSE) reactor for direct conversion of (bi)carbonate to CO. Using a transparent cell with in situ visualization, we reveal that the PSE regulates proton transport, reduces local proton reduction, limits bubble accumulation and facilitates CO2 transport to the cathode. The PEM–PSE reactor achieves a CO Faradaic efficiency of 90% at 200 mA cm−2, a carbon efficiency of 84%, and an energy consumption of ~26.0 GJ t−1 CO. It operates at current densities up to 800 mA cm−2, reaching a CO rate of ~8.0 mmol h−1 cm−2. These results highlight the regulation of proton and gas transport in the electrochemical conversion of captured carbon. Turning captured carbon dioxide into useful chemicals can save energy, but combining capture and conversion is difficult. Here, the authors report a membrane reactor converts bicarbonate solutions directly into carbon monoxide with high carbon efficiency and lower energy use.

title: Strain-engineered fabrication of high-density aligned graphene-based nanoscrolls via UV-tunable adhesive tapes
authors: Maki Nakatani; Akari Sudo; Pablo Solís‐Fernández; Haiming Sun; Satoru Fukamachi; Tomoki MAEZAWA; Tatsuya Ikuta; Takako Matsunaga; Aika Uchida; Masatoshi Mitsuhara; Yung-Chang Lin; Koji Takahashi; Rika Matsumoto; Kazu Suenaga; Takahiro Yamamoto
abstract: Abstract Graphene nanoscrolls (GNSs), one-dimensional nanostructures formed by rolling up a single sheet of graphene, exhibit electronic and mechanical properties distinct from the original graphene sheet. Although several methods have been proposed to synthesize GNSs, achieving high-density GNSs with controlled scroll chirality and direction remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the strain-engineered fabrication of large-scale GNSs using an ultraviolet (UV) light-tunable adhesive tape. The UV tape is stretched to apply tensile strain to graphene stacked on it, and releasing the applied strain by detaching the graphene from the tape results in the formation of GNSs. This strain-assisted method gives isolated GNSs of increased density ( ≈ 380 nanoscrolls per mm) and length (90 μm). This method also allows control of the scroll angle, i.e., chiral angle, by controlling the stretch direction of the tape/graphene stack. The nanoscroll structure allows the intercalation of metal chloride molecules, resulting in an increase of the electrical conductivity. Furthermore, heteronanoscrolls of graphene and MoS 2 are realized by stretching MoS 2 /graphene heterostacks, exhibiting clear optical response. Our controlled synthesis of GNSs and heteronanoscrolls provides an opportunity to manipulate nanomaterials through the strain engineering with the functional UV tape.

title: Regionalized greenhouse gas emissions and infrastructure requirements for future global iron and steel production
authors: Tom Terlouw; Carina Harpprecht; Christian Bauer
abstract: Abstract The steel industry accounts for approximately 7–9% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it a key sector for decarbonization. Here, we quantify current and prospective greenhouse gas emissions from crude steel production facilities worldwide. Based on life cycle assessment, current greenhouse gas emissions of global crude steel production are around 3.7 gigatonnes carbon dioxide equivalent per year, highly concentrated in Asia. Depending on the future 2 ◦ C scenario in 2040, greenhouse gas emissions may decline by up to 70%, to 1.1–2.3 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year. Also, we show that decarbonizing steel may require up to 90 million tonnes of hydrogen per year, 1.0 gigatonne of carbon dioxide storage per year, and/or electricity supply with up to 6,000 terawatt-hours per year, more than twice the European Union’s current electricity supply. Our results highlight the importance of regional context and the substantial infrastructure needs of low-carbon steel production.

title: Kinetic acceleration of phosphate remediation in dilute aquatic environments via photovoltaic-driven solid-state electrolyte electrocoagulation
authors: Shan Liu; Xiaosong Gu; Zhongxin Chen; Jiaxiang Liang; Hong Chen
abstract: The kinetic limitations of reclaiming low-level orthophosphate (PO43−) in low-conductivity natural water bodies impede the in-depth remediation of anthropogenic eutrophication. Conventional adsorption and electrocoagulation (EC) methods are hindered by excessive chemical reagent consumption, high electrical energy demand, and substantial metal electrode consumption. Here, we present a solid-state electrolyte electrocoagulation (SEE) system that employs an interfacial coupling strategy to integrate dynamic ion enrichment with in situ anodic coagulation. By concentrating PO43− at the solid-state electrolyte interface, the system overcomes inherent mass-transport constraints and enhances ion conductivity in dilute media. This localized concentration gradient accelerates apparent reaction kinetics, achieving a removal rate of 0.197 mg/L·min, minimizing energy consumption to 0.0325 kWh/g P and iron consumption to 3.829 g/g P. Consequently, SEE enables efficient, one-step purification below strict regulatory thresholds ( ≤ 0.02 mg/L, China’s Class I Surface Water Environmental Quality Standard). Validated as a photovoltaic-integrated, boat-mounted unit, this approach offers a robust decentralized solution for natural waters, with techno-economic and life cycle assessments confirming its economic viability and low environmental footprint. A solar-powered electrocoagulation system rapidly removes low-level phosphate from natural waters via interfacial ion concentration, overcoming mass-transfer limits for efficient decentralized water purification with low energy and material use.

title: Free tropospheric halogen oxidation drives mercury deposition in the Asia Pacific region
authors: Ju Hyeon Lee; Young-Gwang Kim; Ho‐In Lee; Seung Hyeon Lim; Joël Savarino; Alfonso Saiz‐Lopez; Jeroen E. Sonke; Kitae Kim; Ki‐Tae Park; Eunho Jang; Yeongcheol Han; Aryeh I. Feinberg; Hélène Angot; Ilann Bourgeois; Sae Yun Kwon
abstract: Asian outflow represents 50% of global anthropogenic mercury emissions, but the atmospheric oxidation pathways controlling its deposition to the adjacent Pacific Ocean remain poorly constrained. Using multi-year snow and atmospheric mercury isotope measurements from Mt. Halla, Jeju Island, Korea, we delineate the mercury sources and oxidation pathways governing deposition to marginal Asia and the western Pacific. Mass-independent fractionation of even-number mercury isotopes (even-MIF; Δ 200 Hg) correlates with both air mass transport distance and trajectory altitude, indicating the importance of free tropospheric mercury photo-oxidation triggering even-MIF. Coupled anomalies between Δ 200 Hg and oxygen isotopes of nitrate (Δ 17 O(NO 3 - )) in snow indicate that reactive bromine, generated from debromination of local sea salt aerosol, sustains oxidative capacity in the free troposphere and drives active mercury deposition to Mt. Halla snow. Isotope mixing models quantify that halogen-mediated free tropospheric mercury oxidation (68%) exceeds near-surface oxidation (32%). Our results provide field-based evidence for a bromine-driven free tropospheric photo-oxidation mechanism regulating mercury deposition to Asia-Pacific ecosystems.

title: Identification and genetic characterization of megabase-scale plasmids of Enterobacteriaceae
authors: Allison K. Guitor; Shuai Wang; Owen T. Tuck; Brian Firek; Nadezda Kryuchkova-Mostacci; April A. Jauhal; Lin-Xing Chen; Agata H Dziegiel; Stephen G. Baker; Vu Thuy Duong; Alison E. Mather; Jukka Corander; Anu Kantele; Liat Shenhav; Markus Hilty
abstract: Abstract Humans and animals are ubiquitously colonized by Enterobacteriaceae , including both commensals and clinically significant pathogens. Here, we report 21 complete Enterobacteriaceae megaplasmid genomes of up to 1.58 Mbp in length spanning two major clades that are highly divergent from previously described plasmids. Of these, three were reconstructed from isolates of Escherichia coli and Shigella flexneri ; others were potentially hosted by species of Citrobacter and Enterobacter . Related megabase-scale plasmids were detected in at least 400 infant and adult gut, and other microbiomes. Diverse Enterobacteriaceae hosts, conjugation machinery, and DNA modification patterns suggest that these elements are self-transmissible, with a broad host range. The plasmids encode multi-drug efflux systems and potential secreted effectors. Up to 208 tRNAs are encoded and include sequence variants that may counter tRNA-centric defense mechanisms. Overall, the vast plasmid coding capacity may broaden host range, increase competitiveness, control invasion by other elements, and counter programmed cell death.

title: Divergent anaerobic fates of biodegradable plastics in landfill leachate
authors: Shinhyeong Choe; Hyungmin Choi; Hoseong Moon; Woohyuk Shin; Sunho Park; 박희주; Ju Yong Lee; Sukhwan Yoon; Konstantinos T. Konstantinidis; Changsoo Lee; Jaewook Myung
abstract: Biodegradable plastics (BPs) are increasingly promoted as sustainable alternatives to conventional polymers, yet their fate in landfills remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), in landfill leachate under mesophilic conditions by quantifying carbon conversion to biogas. The BPs exhibited sharply contrasting degradation trajectories: PHB mineralized completely within 17 d, whereas PLA underwent substantial mineralization over 320 d (83.6%), extending beyond the well-established expectation of limited mesophilic degradation. In contrast, PBAT remained largely recalcitrant. Multi-omics analyses linked PHB and PLA depolymerization to the biofilm–polymer interface, with depolymerase transcription tracking their distinct degradation phases. Putative depolymerase homologs were widespread across recovered bacterial genomes, yet only a subset showed transcriptional support. This active fraction included multiple under-characterized lineages outside the taxonomic range of experimentally validated degrader genomes, revealing a marked disconnect between genomic potential and realized activity. Our findings show that anaerobic biodegradation outcomes in landfill leachate cannot be inferred from biodegradability labels or genomic potential alone, but emerge from polymer-specific depolymerization constraints and depolymerase transcription enriched at the biofilm–polymer interface. How different biodegradable plastics break down within landfills, particularly landfill leachate, remain unclear. Here, they evaluated the anaerobic biodegradability of three BPs, polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), poly(lactic acid) (PLA), and poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), using a combination of genome-resolved multi-omics.

title: Balancing the Performance Trade-off of Polymer Blends with Heterogeneously Dispersed Nanodomains via Reactive Processing
authors: Hengti Wang; Chao-Jie Li; Ning He; Toshikazu Miyoshi; Yongjin Li
abstract: Polymer blends are ubiquitous though there are persistent material-property trade-offs, due to the limitation of structural design. Here we report a reactive processing strategy that creates heterogeneously dispersed nano-domains (hDNs) of rubbery ethylene-acrylic ester-glycidyl methacrylate terpolymer (EGMA) in polyoxymethylene (POM) matrix. Pre-reactive blending of EGMA with poly (L-lactide) (PLLA) and subsequent melt processing with POM result in formation of the unique morphology, where PLLA serving as the leveraging forces for opposing uniform distribution via chemical bonds and macro-phase separation by physical associations. The resulting materials exhibited optimized mechanical performance impossible to be acquired with conventional counterparts. This work identifies herein innovates how reactive processing can regulate phase morphology while balancing the trade-off among toughness, ductility, strength and stiffness in multicomponent polymer blends, representing a paradigm shift in narrowing gap between structure and tailor-made property towards pilot plant scale. Polymer blends are ubiquitous though there are persistent material-property trade-offs, due to structural design. Here the authors design multicomponent polymers optimizing the material properties.

title: Transforming electrified railway into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization
authors: Can Wan; Xitong Mu; Zihan He; Hui Liu; Pierre Pinson; Ping Ju; Qianwen Xu
abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing electricity requires vast energy storage capacity worldwide, but constructing dedicated storage assets creates substantial capital, material and embodied carbon burdens. Electrified railways already exchange energy with electricity systems through traction and regenerative braking, but their inherent potential as mechanical energy storage remains unexploited. Here we show that modulation of train operations can transform electrified railways into Electrified Rail-Based Energy Storage. By analyzing 326,034 inter-stop train operations, we estimate its global potential at 190 gigawatts in 2025 and 315–579 gigawatts by 2050. Capacity expansion models for China, Europe and India indicate that it can reduce investment in conventional storage by 11.9–20.0%, corresponding to an extrapolated global value of US$14.9–35.1 billion annually. Without increasing total system cost, electricity systems with this flexible resource could further reduce operational CO 2 emissions by 94.3–258.9 million tonnes per year. Electrified railways can therefore complement conventional storage technologies for electricity system decarbonization.

title: Towards scalable DNA data storage with DNA-SaM codec system
authors: Yu Wang; Jiaxin Xu; Yang Wang; Ziang Nie; Jiaquan Huang; Mingen Li; Yaxin Wu; Yixuan Sun; Shanze Chen; Hui Mei; Zhiwei Qin; Junbiao Dai; Xiaoluo Huang
abstract: The exponential growth of global data volume is driving an urgent need for novel storage medium. Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA), nature’s genetic repository, presents a transformative solution with data storage density and lifespan orders of magnitude higher than conventional media. However, scaling DNA storage has been hindered by the complexity of codec algorithms, the generation of biochemically problematic sequences, and the absence of robust architecture for large-scale data. We present DNA-SaM, a system integrating highly efficient encoding, stringent biochemical constraint checks, and a storage unit distribution paradigm facilitated by a two-tiered indexing architecture. DNA-SaM demonstrates linear encoding time complexity and substantially reduced encoding time compared with representative approaches by in silico analysis. Critically, it proactively excludes sequences such as homopolymer runs, tandem repeats, and potential promoter motifs that could interfere with downstream biochemical processes, showing improved compatibility with in vitro and in vivo applications. It is further validated by practical data storage both in vitro and in vivo with a 100% success rate. On the basis of its encoding scheme and sequence design space, DNA-SaM could theoretically store data exceeding 270 petabytes (PB), marking an advancement in the scalability of DNA-based data storage. Scaling DNA storage is limited by complex codecs, biochemically problematic sequences, and insufficient architecture for large-scale data. Here, the authors present DNA-SaM, integrating efficient encoding, biochemical checks, and a storage unit distribution with a two-tiered indexing architecture.

title: Resolving short-term meteorological variability amplifies projected glacier loss and sea-level rise
authors: Lander Van Tricht; Matthias Huss; Harry Zekollari; Rodrigo Aguayo; Janosch Beer; Marit van Tiel; Alexandra von der Esch; Daniel Farinotti
abstract: Global glacier models typically rely on temperature-index mass balance calculations forced with aggregated meteorological data, limiting their ability to resolve short-term variability. Here, we develop a daily-resolution version of the Global Glacier Evolution Model (GloGEM), which we apply globally and compare against the monthly configuration. Our results show that the daily model more closely reproduces mass balance observations and provides a more detailed representation of glacier runoff. Accounting for short-term meteorological variability leads to systematically greater projected mass loss, with up to 25% greater loss in Svalbard. These differences arise from extreme melt days, precipitation-phase transitions, and surface-type feedbacks not fully represented at monthly resolution. Globally, the daily model yields ice volume losses of 26 ± 10% under low-emission and 47 ± 17% under high-emission scenarios over 2025-2100 (ensemble mean ± 1 StD), resulting in an additional 5-10% mass loss (20-33 mm of global mean sea-level rise) relative to the monthly implementation. Resolving high-frequency forcing, or accounting for its effects through parameterisations, is therefore essential for robust glacier projections, while its omission may systematically underestimate future glacier loss.

title: Polymer-agnostic crosslinking enables robust high-temperature dielectrics for energy storage
authors: Lu Fan; 강효민; Zongliang Xie; Xi Chen; He Li; Shiqi Lai; Ashlin M. Deatherage; Tiffany Chen; Sherrie Qian; Tao Han; Steve W. Shelton; Eric A. Dailing; Myeongjae Lee; Yalin Wang; Jinhui Tao
abstract: Capacitive energy storage under high operating temperatures and electric fields exceeds the limits of most commercial polymers. While crosslinking can, in principle, enhance electro-thermal stability of polymers, conventional approaches remain severely constrained by their reliance on polymer-specific chemistries and often introduce defects that compromise insulation. Herein we present a polymer-agnostic crosslinking platform based on nitrene-mediated C–H insertion, enabling substantial performance and stability improvement across chemically diverse commercial dielectric polymers. Using polyetherimide as a benchmark, the crosslinked film delivers a discharged energy density of 6.0 J cm−3 with >90% efficiency at 200 °C, along with robust cycling stability ( > 1 × 105 cycles) under harsh operational conditions (at 500 MV m−1) and a projected service lifetime of 60 years under standard industrial fields. This work establishes a facile and practical pathway to upgrade existing industrial polymers for reliable operation under harsh environments. In capacitive energy storage systems, crosslinking can improve polymer electrothermal stability, but conventional approaches rely on polymer-specific chemistries and often introduce defects that compromise insulating performance. Here the authors present a polymer-agnostic crosslinking platform based on nitrene mediated C–H insertion that improves performance and stability across a wide range of commercial dielectric polymers.

title: Human targeting of morphologically unique fishes amplifies the risk of functional erosion
authors: P. Bouchet; Sébastien Brosse; Aurèle Toussaint
abstract: Human societies are drawing on wild species for food, fuel, medicines, and recreation. Yet, it remains unclear whether different types of human use target species with common or unique ecological roles. Here we show that humans use a fourth (26%) of the freshwater fish species and these species occupy almost half (45.2%) of the global spectrum of fish morphological diversity. Yet, used species harbour unique trait combinations, that differ according to the way humans use the species such as fisheries, aquaculture, game fish and aquarium. Moreover, the species targeted by humans are characterised by traits that are predominantly associated with threatened species. By simulating the extinction of threatened species used by humans, we revealed a pronounced and non-random erosion of the morphological spectrum. Understanding the trait-based impacts of human use is thus essential to buffer human impact on natural resources. Conservation should therefore safeguard threatened species but also preserve irreplaceable trait combinations that support unique ecological strategies. A quarter of the world’s freshwater fish species are used for food, recreation, or ornamental purposes. These species harbour unique morphologies, many threatened, whose loss would erode irreplaceable ecological strategies.

title: Functional diversity complements taxonomical diversity in productivity-biodiversity relationships in freshwaters
authors: Guohao Liu; Caio Graco‐Roza; Wenfei Liao; Ramiro Martín‐Devasa; Laura Castañeda‐Gómez; Anette Teittinen; Xinxin Qi; Yuying Li; Xiaodong Qu; Mikołaj Kokociński; Naicheng Wu; Janne Soininen
abstract: Abstract Productivity is widely considered a key driver of biodiversity, yet whether taxonomic and functional diversity respond similarly to productivity gradients remains unclear. Using phosphorus as an indicator for productivity gradient, we compiled 78 freshwater datasets spanning > 30,000 sites globally to test how productivity–biodiversity relationships (PBRs) vary across diversity dimensions, trophic groups, and ecosystems. We show that PBRs are predominantly unimodal across taxonomic and functional dimensions, with slightly weaker curvature for functional diversity. Unimodal PBRs are more pronounced in producers than in consumers and show stronger curvature in lakes than in rivers. Functional reorganization also varies along the phosphorus gradient, with the clearest contraction in resource-related trait space and marked shifts in community functional centroids. Climatic, geographic and human land-use gradients further modify PBR shape. These findings indicate that predicting biodiversity responses to productivity benefits from considering functional diversity, ecological context, and broad-scale environmental gradients.

title: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation sustains carbon sinks under warming Tibetan permafrost region
authors: Xu-Ri Xu-Ri; Jiaoneng Yu; Songbo Qu; Tian-Liang; Ribu Shama; Haojing Lei; Yuxuan Cui; Xingliang Xu; Yude Pan; Haishan Niu; Almaz Borjigidai; Eryuan Liang; Fahu Chen
abstract: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation (SNF) by legumes is a major natural source of reactive nitrogen that supports ecosystem functioning and carbon sequestration. Warming across the Tibetan Plateau alpine permafrost region may trigger substantial shifts in vegetation composition and distribution, yet the consequences for ecosystem nitrogen inputs remain poorly understood. Here, using 1047 plant samples from 323 plots across the Tibetan Plateau and 15N natural-abundance techniques, we quantify legume and non-legume nitrogen sources and regional aboveground SNF rates. Aboveground SNF is tightly linked to legume aboveground biomass, ranges from 0 to 7.43 g N m−2 yr−1, and peaks at elevations of 3600–4000 m. At the regional scale, its spatial distribution largely coincides with recent decadal gains in aboveground biomass and plant nitrogen density. Process-based simulations show that removing SNF causes severe nitrogen limitation and shifts these ecosystems from a carbon sink to a source. Our findings highlight the important role of legumes in sustaining carbon sinks in Tibetan Plateau permafrost ecosystems. Aboveground symbiotic nitrogen fixation by legumes provides a critical nitrogen source that supports plant biomass growth and sustains carbon sequestration in warming Tibetan permafrost grasslands, based on nitrogen isotope analyses and ecosystem modeling.

title: Unlocking electric vehicle flexibility in microgrids via lightweight on-charger coordination
authors: Yehui Li; Xueyuan Cui; Chongqing Kang; Thomas Morstyn; Yue Wang
abstract: The large-scale integration of electric vehicles could provide substantial flexibility for balancing renewable energy in microgrids, yet this potential remains largely constrained by uncoordinated charging. Here, we show that on-board chargers can be transformed into intelligent agents to unlock this flexibility through distributed vehicle-grid coordination. To enable such coordination under practical hardware constraints, we develop a distributed framework that embeds edge intelligence into resource-constrained chargers for autonomous charging optimization. Validated on a high-fidelity hardware-in-the-loop platform capturing microgrid cyber-physical dynamics, experimental results demonstrate that our framework reduces memory consumption by 96.1% and communication overhead by 74.3% compared to the traditional distributed coordination scheme. Moreover, unlocking this hardware-level flexibility achieves a 10.8% profit increase over the current uncoordinated situation. Importantly, the proposed framework promises profound economic, environmental, and social benefits for the future energy landscape from 2025 to 2040. Uncoordinated electric vehicle charging strains microgrids, yet advanced control exceeds charger hardware limits. Here, the authors develop a lightweight on-charger coordination framework that unlocks vehicle flexibility with low memory and communication needs.
